'''Bertram Oliver "Bert" Fraser-Reid''' (23 February 1934 – 25 May 2020) was a Jamaican synthetic [[organic chemistry|organic chemist]] who has been widely recognised for his work using [[carbohydrates]] as starting materials for [[Chirality (chemistry)|chiral]] materials and on the role of [[oligosaccharides]] in [[immune response]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Bertram Fraser-Reid |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/heraldsun/name/bertram-fraser-reid-obituary?pid=196325385 |publisher=The News and Observer & Herald Su |access-date=4 September 2021}}</ref> He developed the [[Glycosyl donor|“armed-disarmed” principle]]'''.'''<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020 |title=Bertram Fraser-Reid Obituary (2020) |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/heraldsun/name/bertram-fraser-reid-obituary?id=8726815 |access-date=13 February 2025 |website=Legacy.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024 |title=Armed/disarmed strategy/effect |url=https://chempedia.info/info/armed_disarmed_strategy_effect/ |access-date=13 February 2025 |website=chempedia.info}}</ref>

==Early life==
Fraser-Reid was born in [[Coleyville]], Jamaica to William, an elementary school principal, and Laura, a teacher.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Black scientists|last=Lisa.|first=Yount|date=1991|publisher=Facts on File|isbn=0816025495|location=New York|oclc=22596416}}</ref> He had five older siblings.<ref name=":0" /> Laura died when Fraser-Reid was only nine months old.<ref name=":0" /> He attended [[Excelsior High School (Jamaica)|Excelsior High School]] and [[Clarendon College (Jamaica)|Clarendon College]] before moving to Canada to earn BSc (1959) and MSc (1961) at [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] in [[Ontario]]<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.answers.com/topic/bert-fraser-reid|title=Fraser-Reid Biography |publisher=[[Answers.com]]|access-date=16 November 2007}}</ref> He went to [[University of Alberta]]<ref name=":0" /> to earn a PhD in 1964<ref name=":0" /> under the supervision of [[Raymond Lemieux]]. He went to [[Imperial College London]] to do [[postdoctoral]] work for Nobel Laureate [[Sir Derek Barton]] from 1964 to 1966.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="blackpast">{{cite web|url=http://www.blackpast.org/?q=aah/fraser-reid-bertram-o-1934 |title=The Black Past: Remembered and Reclaimed: Fraser-Reid |date=18 January 2007 |publisher=[[BlackPast.org]], [[University of Washington]], Seattle|access-date=16 November 2007}}</ref>

==Academic career==
From 1966 to 1980 Fraser-Reid was on the faculty of the [[University of Waterloo]] in [[Waterloo, Ontario]]<ref name=":0" /> where he established a research group known as "Fraser-Reid's Rowdies".<ref name="panorama">{{cite web|first=Jaevion |last=Nelson |url=http://fr.takingitglobal.org/express/panorama/article.html?ContentID=5431|title=Panorama: Let Us Honour a Great Man|date=20 April 2005|access-date=16 November 2007}}</ref> The primary emphasis of his work at this point was the synthesis of [[Chirality (chemistry)|chiral]] natural products using [[carbohydrates]] as the starting materials. In 1975, Fraser-Reid was the first to publish a method for making nonsugar compounds with simple sugars.<ref name=":0" /> In 1980, he was hired at the [[University of Maryland, College Park]],<ref name=":0" /> and then at [[Duke University]] in [[North Carolina]] in 1983.<ref name=":0" /> In 1985 he was appointed the [[James B. Duke Professor]] of Chemistry.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite book|url=http://www.bookrags.com/biography/bertram-oliver-fraser-reid-woc/|title=Fraser-Reid biography |publisher=[[BookRags]] |access-date=20 November 2007}}</ref> At Duke University, his research shifted to exploring the role of [[oligosaccharides]] in immune responses, and particularly on the effect of molecules on human diseases like [[malaria]] and [[AIDS]]. After retiring from Duke in 1996, due to an undisclosed harassment claim,<ref>{{cite news |first=Justin |last=Dillon |title=Professor retires amid harassment allegations |url=http://www.dukechronicle.com/article/professor-retires-amid-harassment-allegations |publisher=[[The Chronicle Online]], The Independent Daily at Duke University |date=31 May 1995 |access-date=19 September 2012 }}</ref> he established the Natural Products & Glycotechnology Research Institute, a nonprofit, to study the carbohydrate chemistry/biology of tropical [[parasitic diseases]] in developing countries and to develop a carbohydrate-based [[malaria vaccine]].<ref name="blackpast"/> Fraser-Reid and his team achieved a milestone in oligosaccharide synthesis by assembling a molecule consisting of 28 [[monosaccharide]] units.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/news/84/i46/8446carbs.html| title=Largest Synthetic Hetero-Oligosaccharide |publisher=[[Chemical and Engineering News]]|date=8 November 2006|access-date=20 November 2007}}</ref>

==Achievements==
Several sources have reported that Fraser-Reid was nominated in 1998 for a Nobel Prize in chemistry for his work on oligosaccharides and immune responses.<ref name="panorama"/><ref name="gleaner">{{cite news
 |first=Ross
 |last=Sheil
 |title=The sugar doctor
 |url=http://www.jamaica-gleaner.com/gleaner/20070117/lead/lead4.html
 |publisher=[[Jamaica Gleaner]]
 |date=17 January 2007 |access-date=16 November 2007 |url-status=dead
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071215202147/http://jamaica-gleaner.com/gleaner/20070117/lead/lead4.html
 |archive-date=15 December 2007
}}</ref><ref name="musgrave"/> This statement cannot be verified since the names of the nominees are never publicly announced, and neither are they told that they have been considered for the Prize. [[Nobel Prize#Selection|Nomination records]] are sealed for fifty years.

The [[Institute of Jamaica]] awarded Fraser-Reid the 2007 [[Musgrave Medal]] (Gold) for his work in chemistry, noting that during his career he co-authored over 330 [[peer-reviewed]] publications and supervised 85 [[Postdoctoral researcher|post-doctoral fellows]] and 55 PhD students.<ref name="musgrave">{{cite web| url=http://www.instituteofjamaica.org.jm/Docs/citations07/BERT_FRASER_citation.pdf| title=Musgrave Medal Citation| access-date=20 November 2007| archive-date=4 February 2022| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220204121646/https://instituteofjamaica.org.jm/Docs/citations07/BERT_FRASER_citation.pdf/| url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Other interests==
Along with his interest in science, Fraser-Reid was a pianist and organist who gave recitals at venues such as St. George's Cathedral, Kingston, Jamaica (December 1986) and [[Seville Cathedral|Cathedral de Seville]], Spain (August 1995).<ref name="musgrave"/>

In the 1970s Fraser-Reid filed a lawsuit against a building contractor who had not followed municipal building codes. The case went all the way to the [[Supreme Court of Canada]] where Fraser-Reid prevailed, and "Fraser-Reid v Droumtsekas" is often cited in [[Law of Canada|Canadian civil law]].
<ref>{{cite web|url=https://scc-csc.lexum.com/scc-csc/scc-csc/en/item/4483/index.do|title=Fraser-Reid v. Droumtsekas|publisher=[[Supreme Court of Canada]]|access-date=16 June 2020}}</ref>
